sources.author: Swyx (Shawn Wang)
sources.headline: Founder @ Latent Space | AI Engineer, ex-Netlify, ex-AWS
sources.post_summary: Shared a breakdown of why most 'AI agent' demos fail in production — the gap isn't the LLM, it's the lack of deterministic guardrails around tool calls. Cited three internal postmortems from AI infra teams. The thread resonated because it named the dirty secret nobody posts about: agents that look great in demos are flaky at p95.

sources.author: Cassie Kozyrkov
sources.headline: Chief Decision Scientist | AI Strategy | ex-Google | Keynote Speaker
sources.post_summary: Posted a hot take: 'The companies winning with AI agents right now aren't using the fanciest models — they're the ones who spent 6 months on evals.' Included a simple 2x2 grid showing model quality vs. eval rigor and where most enterprise rollouts fail. Struck a nerve with CTOs and ML platform teams.

sources.author: Tom Donahue
sources.headline: Founding Engineer @ stealth AI infra | prev Staff SWE @ Stripe | building in public
sources.post_summary: Detailed how his team replaced a 400-line Python orchestration script with a Claude Code agent running inside a GitHub Action — cut setup time from 2 days to 45 minutes per new microservice. Shared the exact prompt structure and the one gotcha (context window blowout on large diffs) that burned them twice before they fixed it.

sources.author: Sarah Guo
sources.headline: Founder @ Conviction | Investor in AI infrastructure | prev Greylock
sources.post_summary: Argued that the next infra bottleneck for AI agents isn't compute or context — it's identity and permissions. 'Your agent needs a passport, not just an API key.' Called out the whitespace between OAuth, service accounts, and the emerging agentic identity layer, and named three startups quietly building in this space.

sources.author: Kyle Coleman
sources.headline: CMO at Clari | Revenue Intelligence | GTM Strategy
sources.post_summary: AI SDRs are not replacing human reps — they're exposing which reps were never doing real work. The teams seeing 3x pipeline from AI outbound aren't cutting headcount. They're freeing their best reps to do the 20% of work that actually closes deals. The math is simple: AI handles volume, humans handle judgment.

sources.author: Vin Matano
sources.headline: B2B Content Strategist | Helping GTM teams build pipelines with content | Creator Economy for Sales
sources.post_summary: I analyzed 90 days of outbound campaigns across 12 SaaS companies. The ones with the highest reply rates all had one thing in common: they led with a specific trigger, not a persona. 'I saw you just hired 3 AEs' outperforms 'VP of Sales at a Series B company' every single time. Signal-led > ICP-led.

sources.author: Natalie Furness
sources.headline: RevOps Consultant | Founder at RevOps Automated | Helping B2B SaaS scale without the chaos
sources.post_summary: Your CRM is lying to you. Not because someone entered bad data — because your pipeline stages don't reflect buyer behavior, they reflect what your sales team is comfortable admitting. Stage 3 doesn't mean 'Champion identified.' It means 'rep doesn't want to move it back to Stage 1.' Fix your stage definitions before you fix your data.

sources.author: Tom Lavery
sources.headline: CEO at Jiminny | Conversation Intelligence | Helping revenue teams unlock insights from every customer interaction
sources.post_summary: Content is now the new cold call. The reps hitting quota in 2026 have a LinkedIn presence that warms every outbound touch before it lands. Buyers Google your name before they reply to your email. If your profile is a resume, you're starting every deal 20% behind. Build in public or get outcompeted by someone who does.

sources.author: Priya Nair
sources.headline: Indie hacker | Built 3 products, 1 profitable | ex-Google PM
sources.post_summary: Priya shared that her AI-powered SOW generator hit $12k MRR after 8 months of building nights and weekends. She broke down the exact moment she stopped adding features and started talking to customers — and how that single shift doubled her conversion rate in 6 weeks.

sources.author: Marcus Webb
sources.headline: Laid off → shipped my first app in 90 days | Claude API + Next.js | DM me if you're in the same boat
sources.post_summary: Marcus documented his entire journey from a January layoff at a Fortune 500 to launching a B2B tool for freelance contractors — with zero prior coding background. The post resonated because he was brutally honest: the first two ideas flopped, he almost quit in week 6, and the version that got traction looked nothing like his original plan.

sources.author: Sione Tuilagi
sources.headline: Full-stack dev | Shipping in public | $0 → $3k MRR in 4 months
sources.post_summary: Sione posted a raw screenshot comparing his week 1 commit history (3 commits, all README edits) to week 16 (47 commits, first paying customer). No motivational spin — just the actual diff. He called out the specific week he wanted to delete the repo and why he didn't. Developers and first-time builders flooded the comments with their own inflection-point stories.

sources.author: Elena Marchetti
sources.headline: Former teacher → Software engineer | 2 years in | Writing about the gap nobody talks about
sources.post_summary: Elena's post called out the specific skills bootcamps don't teach: reading other people's spaghetti code, estimating timelines honestly, and the art of the good-enough PR. She framed it as a letter to her bootcamp self, but the point of view was sharp enough that senior engineers were sharing it as onboarding reading material.
